Sexual dysfunction

Short-term outcomes are mixed across small studies. A pelvic-floor trial found no added benefit from PBM over vaginal stretching alone, while other cause-specific studies report changes in sexual-function scores or pain.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Sexual-function score — Cassano et al. 2019 reported a greater decrease in SAFTEE-SI symptoms with transcranial PBM than sham in 20 participants: −2.55 ± 1.88 versus −0.45 ± 1.21 (p = 0.011). Twelve participants completed the trial.

Pelvic-floor myofascial pain — Frederice et al. 2022 found short-term improvement with vaginal stretching both with and without PBM. Only the sham group showed significant improvement in total FSFI and desire scores, with no clear added effect from PBM.

Breast-cancer hormone-therapy symptoms — Vieira and Rezende 2026 reported within-group changes after PBM: vaginal-pain VAS 9.46 to 1.04 and QS-F scores 23.25 to 87.21. Treatment was self-selected and the comparison was not randomized.

Vulvovaginal symptoms after cancer treatment — Forret et al. 2023 reported that 18 participants felt better or much better after PBM in an uncontrolled cohort.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low certainty for short-term sexual-function and dyspareunia outcomes in the studied groups. Findings are mixed across a small transcranial trial analysis and a sham-controlled pelvic-floor trial (Cassano et al. 2019; Frederice et al. 2022).

The mouse findings provide very low-certainty evidence for human outcomes (Liu et al. 2025).

Summary of the Evidence

Small clinical studies report changes in sexual-function scores or pain for selected groups, but the findings are mixed. A pelvic-floor trial found no added benefit from PBM over vaginal stretching alone, while a small depression-trial analysis favored transcranial PBM. Uncontrolled studies report larger changes in breast-cancer-related symptoms, but evidence does not yet show a consistent effect across causes.

Human and clinical evidence

A secondary analysis of a double-blind depression trial included 20 participants receiving near-infrared transcranial PBM or sham. The active group had a larger short-term improvement in sexual-function scores. Twelve participants completed the trial, and sexual function was an exploratory secondary outcome rather than the primary endpoint (Cassano et al. 2019).

In a double-blind randomized trial of 103 women with pelvic-floor myofascial pain, vaginal stretching was paired with either 808-nm PBM or sham PBM. Both groups improved in painful intercourse and in the proportion meeting the study threshold for sexual dysfunction. The PBM group did not show a clear additional benefit over sham; only the sham group had significant gains in total sexual-function and desire scores (Frederice et al. 2022).

A prospective study of women with breast-cancer hormone-therapy symptoms compared 24 women who chose PBM with eight observational controls. After four sessions over four weeks, the PBM group reported lower vaginal-pain scores and higher sexual-function scores. Self-selection, unequal groups, and non-random allocation limit interpretation of the large within-group changes (Vieira and Rezende 2026).

A separate prospective cohort of women with vulvovaginal symptoms after cancer treatment reported that 18 participants felt better or much better after PBM. With no control group, the study cannot determine how much change was caused by treatment (Forret et al. 2023).

Animal evidence

In male mice exposed to chronic restraint stress, transcranial near-infrared PBM improved low-sexual-desire and depression-related behavioral measures. The study linked these changes to activity markers in hypothalamic dopaminergic neurons. This result does not establish effects in people (Liu et al. 2025).

A 2022 comprehensive narrative review examined transcranial PBM for sexual dysfunction associated with depression or antidepressant medication. It predates the later pelvic-floor and breast-cancer studies and provides no pooled effect estimate (Salehpour et al. 2022).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The depression study used 823-nm transcranial LED treatment for 20–30 minutes twice weekly over eight weeks. The pelvic-floor trial used 808-nm near-infrared PBM at three vaginal points during ten stretching sessions. The breast-cancer study used local 440-nm blue and 660-nm red light over four sessions. These protocols target different tissues and causes, so their results do not establish one transferable schedule or device.

Interpretation

The human evidence includes a small exploratory signal, a larger sham-controlled trial without a clear PBM-specific advantage, and uncontrolled improvements in cancer-related symptoms. The mouse result is a cause-specific preclinical observation. Larger trials should test separate populations with prespecified sexual-function outcomes and follow-up long enough to assess durability.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The small depression trial treated sexual function as a secondary outcome, while the pelvic-floor trial found improvements with vaginal stretching both with and without PBM (Cassano et al. 2019; Frederice et al. 2022). Breast-cancer symptom studies were not randomized (Vieira and Rezende 2026; Forret et al. 2023). The varied populations, outcomes, and short follow-up limit confidence in a general or lasting effect.
